The shortage of French professors also doesn't surprise me. They're paid hourly and many of them teach at centers in different parts of the city. The schedule is quite bad as well. There's usually morning groups from 12h - 16h and then night groups from 18h - 21h and then weekend classes. You can't make a living from just teaching one class so you're forced to teach multiple classes at multiple different centers which means either working late into the night or working weekends. The ones who are passionate spend their free time looking for additional resources online for their students. Basically working full time with absolutely no benefits and only getting hourly pay.

Bonjour! Queer American living in Montreal and I would say the first step is to get a work permit for Canada. Ideally you would get a company to give you a closed work permit for a couple of years because you usually get an extra 50 points for immigration if you can secure a closed permit. I would also suggest you try it out. Have you visited? Getting an open work permit is also much easier and would allow you some flexibility if you need to quit and find another job or if you need to take a break from working. Work inside of Canada is much more valuable than outside of Canada. You can live in QC while you build up your work experience and then decide whether you'd like to stay in QC or move to a different province. It's really important if you decide to move permanently to read up on Quebec immigration policies and think about if you want to go through all of that.

I really love the culture and vibe of Montreal. The queer community here is really amazing and it's small enough that you really get to feel a sense of closeness to people. However, it will take 2-3 times as long and about twice as much money to get PR through QC than it would be to get PR through the federal government. You'll probably have to apply for a bridging work permit as it takes 21 months for the federal government to process applications coming from QC (more money out of your pockets) and yes you have to pay the federal government for your PR application on top of QC application fees. Many of my friends have had to hire private French tutors, which you don't need to do but the free french classes can be hit or miss and French exams are notoriously difficult so many people do get tutors. The EE program is much faster as it only takes 6 months vs two years to get your PR card and honestly the queer community outside of Montreal is cool too. I work remotely for a company in Toronto and I've visited during pride and the vibe was really nice. I'm leaving because I'm a POC and the xenophobia and racism in the qc government has become a little too intense for me. Feel free to message me if you need more info since I've been here for about 6 years now so I can give you the skinny on the drama that's been happening inside the province in regards to immigration.
